newsitem.title: UK: DMG case focuses on dilemma of star fund managers.
newsitem.headline: DMG case focuses on dilemma of star fund managers.

text.p: Where do you go if you're a top fund manager on a million a year, but the job satisfaction derived from challenge and responsibility still eludes you?
The suspension of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's star manager Nicola Horlick reveals a testing dilemma for industry high flyers, fund industry sources say.

Horlick, head of DMG's 18 billion stg UK pension fund division, was suspended on Tuesday for "possible breach of contract" after she was discovered planning to jump ship and take some of her 30-strong team and clients with her.
"This is not just a protocol problem," said a London fund manager who declined to be named. "She's obviously a talented manager looking for somewhere to grow her career."
"She was doing what most of the top dogs spend most of their time doing -- looking for their next lucrative package," said another. "She just got caught."

He suggested the "highly political" suspension would reflect poorly on DMG, who last year swooped to poach an entire Latin American team of analysts from ING Barings. Such moves, which tend to boost pay packages, may be resented by employers but are a favourite self-advancement tactic for high-fliers.
Usually the secretly-planned defection of an individual or a team is a fait accompli, achieved before the costly and unsettling exodus can be stopped.
Press reports claim clients approached by Horlick revealed her intended move to DMG. Now, investment houses are increasingly insisting on contracts which block that option.
Horlick has not confirmed publicly whether she was attempting to move or why, but ABN-Amro, the Dutch bank named as her possible employer, has denied attempting to poach DMG staff.

Both DMG and the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation (IMRO) insist the suspension is nothing to do with the sacking last year of another big name, Peter Young, although Horlick knew him from Mercury Asset Management where both had previously worked.
Fund consultants said managers typically climb the career ladder by handling more assets on an increasingly global basis.

Marketing departments sell funds to clients on the back of the skills and track record of the managers -- Horlick is known to have pulled in a record amount of UK pension fund money for DMG in the last two years, and has outperformed her peers.

"But what sometimes happens is that good fund managers who love the buzz of the markets find that as they become more senior, management duties rather than pure investment decisions dominate their job," said one consultant. "They don't want it." He noted that a series of scandals in recent years had also resulted in more scrutiny from nervous trustees, investment committees and regulators, especially where retail money or assets for vulnerable groups like pensioners are concerned.
At the same time managers are under relentless pressure to produce ever-higher returns.

Senior fund managers in some big organisations feel they are hemmed in by committee decisions and are opting to switch to a smaller organisation where they take the decisions and the responsibility, or set up a "boutique" for select clients.

The trend started among hedge funds in the 1980s, when young managers left George Soros, Michael Seinhardt or Julian Robertson to set up on their own, the consultant said. The same drift has since affected traditional equity investment houses like Fidelity, Barings and Schroders.

The latest is Fidelity's Boston-based Michael Gray, who controls $10 billion in nine mutual funds and aims to start his own investment management firm. He follows Larry Greenberg, who managed $21 billion but felt he was not being paid enough.
